#### Suspense Fluency

The Suspense fluency is how Suspense works, as a harness working in any project needs to know it to talk about it or write for it: what the modes are and what each may change, how a Chain prompt runs, how prompts and questions are handed back to the user, and what the application adds to a prompt of its own accord. Every mode but Freeform is pointed at it, so a question asked to write a Chain prompt, or a task asked about the queue, knows what that is, in a project that says nothing of Suspense itself. Like the Piton fluency, it is never part of the system prompt, so the prompt cache holds whatever the mode.
It is the same for every project, and is the application's own, not a project's to edit: its source is a Markdown file in this application's own repository, `suspense-fluency.md` in its `.suspense/system-prompts` directory beside the defaults, baked into the application when it is built, as they are, so a build always ships with whatever it says, and a build can't be made without it. It is not among the prompts a project saves or the [SettingsWindowScope](../../settings-window/index.md#settings-window-scope) edits.
It is written to the Suspense fluency file, `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in the project's data, as the [ProjectDataScope](../../project-data/index.md#project-data-scope) says, before any Code, Chain, Spec, or Ask prompt is compiled, whenever the file isn't there or doesn't hold what the application ships, so it keeps in step with the application rather than the project. It is written as text, never read as Piton, holds no placeholder and no path of the machine it was written on, and so reads the same on the host and in a container.
It says, plainly and briefly, written for a harness rather than for the user, each of these in a short paragraph of its own.
- that Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code, and that a prompt is sent to the harness in one of five modes, in the order and with the meanings the PromptModesScope gives: Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is, Chain changes the spec and then the code to match, Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is, Ask asks a question and changes nothing, and Freeform passes a prompt to the harness exactly as typed
- that Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks, run in a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each, queueing behind tasks of their own lane, and that questions run at once and never queue

# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user reads, edits, answers, and sends; neither is ever sent by itself.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.

+- An Ask prompt is a question.

Code, Chain, Spec and Ask prompts are now pointed at a Suspense fluency file that explains how Suspense works; Freeform never is. The full test suite passes (508). I haven't sent a prompt through the running app with it.

**What Suspense writes:** the source is `.suspense/system-prompts/suspense-fluency.md` in this repo, baked into the app, so a build fails without it (`src/suspense_fluency.rs`). Before any Code, Chain, Spec or Ask prompt is compiled, it writes that text to `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` in the project if the file is missing or different. The text covers the eight points the spec lists, from the five modes to cancel, resend and new conversation. It names no project or harness and has no placeholders or machine paths.

**How prompts point at it:**
- **Placeholder:** `${SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE}` is filled with `.suspense/suspense-fluency.md`. If the file couldn't be written, the paragraph naming it is dropped, the same as for the Piton fluency.
- **System prompt:** it never mentions the file, so the prompt cache isn't affected.
- **Defaults:** I added the spec's paragraph to `code.md`, `combined.md`, `spec.md` and `ask.md`, right after what each mode is for.
- **This repo:** those files are both the app's defaults and this project's own saved prompts, so this project's prompts point at it from now on.

**Containers, project data and settings:**
- Spec runs and questions mount the file read only.
- New projects' `.gitignore` lists it.
- The System prompts blurb in Settings explains `SUSPENSE_FLUENCY_FILE`.

**One change you didn't ask for:** a test wrote the file into this repo, so I added `/.suspense/suspense-fluency.md` to this repo's own `.gitignore`, next to `fluency.md`. The spec says it belongs to one machine.

**Existing projects still need a reset.** As the spec step said, a project's saved mode prompts don't change when a default changes. The other project you have in mind will only point its Ask at the fluency after you reset its Ask prompt in Settings, or paste in the paragraph by hand. Until then, the fluency file still gets written there; it just isn't mentioned in its prompts.

The spec and the prompt agree.
